title: Paytm Shares Slide as NPCI Confirms 0.4% UPI Fee Above Rs 2,000
excerpt: India's payments authority will levy the first-ever merchant fee on high-value UPI transactions from October 15, a day after the government shielded smaller payments from charges — and investors are repricing Paytm's earnings power.
body:
• The National Payments Corporation of India will levy a 0.4% fee on UPI payments to merchants above Rs 2,000 starting October 15 — the first merchant charge ever imposed on the network, Reuters reported.
  • A government gazette notification issued Monday bars banks and payment system providers from imposing any charge, direct or indirect, on UPI transactions or RuPay debit card payments of up to Rs 2,000.
  • Shares of One 97 Communications, Paytm's parent, fell more than 2.5% to Rs 1,761.80 on the NSE on Tuesday, one session after the stock hit a fresh 52-week high of Rs 1,840.
  • Brokerages are bullish on the shift: Jefferies holds a Buy with a Rs 2,100 target and Bernstein names Paytm its top pick with a Rs 2,200 target, citing MDR as an earnings driver.

A line in the sand at Rs 2,000

India's experiment with entirely free digital payments is about to end — at least for bigger purchases. The National Payments Corporation of India said on Tuesday it would introduce a 0.4% fee on payments to merchants above Rs 2,000 on its UPI network, effective October 15, according to Reuters. The announcement came a day after a finance ministry gazette notification directed that no bank or payment system provider may levy any charge, directly or indirectly, on a person making or receiving a UPI payment or RuPay debit card payment of up to Rs 2,000.

The two moves draw a clean line: small payments stay free, larger merchant transactions enter a fee regime. Shares of One 97 Communications, Paytm's parent, dropped more than 2.5% to Rs 1,761.80 on the NSE on Tuesday morning — one session after the stock hit a fresh 52-week high of Rs 1,840, nearly double its March low of Rs 930.60.

How India got here

The legal groundwork was laid in August, when Parliament passed the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026, amending Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. The law replaced a blanket ban on charges with a framework letting the government specify, by notification, which payment modes stay protected. Monday's notification was the first use of that power — and it deliberately stopped short of protecting payments above Rs 2,000.

The government says the shift is about survival, not revenue. With transaction volumes growing exponentially, the system needs continuous upgrades in cybersecurity, fraud prevention and infrastructure, it said in a statement. "Reliance on subsidies alone is not viable for the next wave of growth," the statement added, calling for a self-sustaining revenue model to keep UPI "robust, inclusive and future-ready."

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has repeatedly clarified that any merchant discount rate would apply to merchants, not end-users, and only to a limited set of transactions above a specified threshold at rates "substantially below typical debit or credit-card MDR." Person-to-person transfers will stay free. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra put the trade-off more bluntly in August.

"Someone has to pay the cost."

— Sanjay Malhotra, RBI Governor, on digital-payments infrastructure

The numbers explain the urgency. UPI processed 2,366 crore transactions worth ₹29.9 lakh crore in July 2026 alone, according to the Press Information Bureau, making it the world's largest real-time payments system. It is now live in 11 foreign countries. The government has reaffirmed that UPI "will remain free for citizens" — but citizens, in this formulation, means people making everyday payments, not the merchants receiving them.

What it means for Paytm

For Paytm, the fee regime could be the monetization unlock analysts have been waiting for. Jefferies recently raised its price target to Rs 2,100 from Rs 1,600 while maintaining a Buy call, arguing Paytm "stands out on monetisation of its client base in near-zero MDR regime, which is now changing favourably." The brokerage points to the fintech's 4.9 crore merchant base and strong loan-origination model, projecting 25% revenue CAGR over FY26-29 alongside a sharp rise in EBITDA and profit. It lifted FY28-29 earnings estimates by 20-25% to factor in 25 basis points of UPI MDR.

Bernstein went further, naming Paytm its top pick with a Rs 2,200 target and FY29 EPS of Rs 78 — Rs 54 even excluding any MDR impact, above the Rs 46 consensus.

The risks are real: merchants may steer customers away from UPI for large tickets, and rivals like PhonePe and Google Pay will fight for the same fee pool.

Diaspora angle

For NRIs, the change is background noise — until they visit India. UPI is the default way returning diaspora pay for everything from taxis to restaurant bills, and a 0.4% merchant fee above Rs 2,000 could quietly surface in pricing at larger retailers.

What to watch

The NPCI-led steering committee still has to publish the full MDR framework, and banks and payment providers will set their own commercial terms around the 0.4% anchor. Watch Paytm's next quarterly commentary for how aggressively it plans to pass through or absorb the fee — and whether merchants, given a choice, stick with UPI or nudge big-ticket buyers back toward cards.

nri_angle: NRIs who use UPI during India visits and diaspora investors in Indian fintech will feel the pricing and valuation shifts as the fee regime takes effect.
